## 1. What was read

**800 research articles** from 33 of the 33 journals on the roster.

A further **127** records (14% of the 927 this month's harvest returned) carry no abstract and are not research: news, correspondence, editor highlights and obituaries. PubMed types them `Journal Article` and nothing else, so the publication-type filter cannot see them — across the whole index they are 22.7% of it and 35% of `general`, and 3,801 of them are JAMA. Every count below is over the full harvest and is inflated by this; the figure above is not.

| General | Cancer | Immune | Bioinfo | Sysbio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 389 | 134 | 84 | 294 | 26 |

!!! warning "Volume swing against the median month: cancer -28%"
    Check the source before reading anything into this. Two benign causes account for most of these. `bioinfo` every January carries the Nucleic Acids Research database issue and runs high. And several journals simply deposit nothing in some months: across the 44 months read, 4 of 33 journals are absent from at least one, worst being *Nat Mach Intell* (20 months missing, 81 papers in total) and *Bioinformatics* (4 months missing, 2,905 papers in total). Every journal on the roster contributed this month. Queried directly, PubMed returns zero for those journal-months too — the holes are in the source, reproduced exactly by re-running the harvest. So a swing here is not evidence that a field went quiet, and is not usually evidence that the pipeline broke either.

Largest contributors: Bioinformatics 109, Nature 102, Nucleic Acids Res 89, Science 77, Lancet 43, JAMA 38.

## 3. The evidence that moved it












**Hallucination detection lands in *Nature*.** [38898292](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38898292/): detecting
hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy. The December
2025 briefing calls auditing a generative model's own output — rather than its
training or its benchmarks — "a new category". It is in *Nature* eighteen months
earlier. This is the fifth first-appearance claim in this corpus to move earlier
on extension, and at this point the individual corrections matter less than the
rule: **first appearance is a property of the window.**

**Two acetylcholine papers, same journal, same month.** [38744292](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38744292/) and
[38744291](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38744291/) (*Immunity*): tuft-cell acetylcholine released into the gut lumen
to promote anti-helminth immunity, and tuft-cell-derived acetylcholine driving
epithelial chloride secretion and helminth clearance. With [38772371](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38772371/)
(*Cell*) — innervation of nociceptor neurons in the spleen promoting
germinal-centre responses — June 2024 has nerves controlling a lymphoid organ and
a named neurotransmitter doing immune work, in the corpus's top venues, in one
month.

## 4. Refutations

### (a) Landing on a tracked thread

Nothing this month lands a refutation on a tracked thread, and that is worth
recording rather than padding. The month's refutations are all methodological.

### (b) Method credibility

[38886757](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38886757/) (*Genome Biol*): beyond benchmarking, towards predictive models
of dataset-specific pipeline performance. The claim is that a benchmark ranking
does not transfer between datasets — which, if true, undercuts the evidentiary
value of the benchmark papers that fill this journal every month, including
[37537502](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37537502/) in the same month systematically benchmarking single-cell ATAC
protocols.

[38940140](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38940140/): BioCoder, a benchmark for bioinformatics code generation with
LLMs. The corpus's July 2026 briefing treats the arrival of benchmarks as the
maturity signal for the agentic thread. Here the benchmark arrives alongside the
capability rather than after it, which weakens benchmarks-as-maturity-signal as
a general reading.
